drills.q: State the LEGB order and identify which scope is searched first vs last.
drills.a: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in, in that order — Local is searched first, Built-in last; lookup stops at the first scope containing the name.

drills.q: A function reads a variable x on line 1 and assigns to x on line 3. Is x treated as local for line 1? Why?
drills.a: Yes. The compiler scans the entire function body for assignments before execution; any assignment anywhere makes the name local for the whole function, including lines textually before the assignment. Line 1 will raise UnboundLocalError at runtime.

drills.q: Predict the output: `funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]; print([f() for f in funcs])`. Explain the mechanism, not just the answer.
drills.a: [2, 2, 2]. All three lambdas close over the same cell object for the loop variable i (not a value snapshotted at creation time); after the loop finishes, that shared cell holds 2, and every lambda reads it when called.

drills.q: Give two independent fixes for the late-binding closure trap and explain the mechanism each relies on.
drills.a: 1) lambda i=i: i — default argument values are evaluated once, at function-definition time, immediately capturing the current value instead of deferring to the shared cell. 2) A factory function def make(i): return lambda: i — each call creates a genuinely new local scope (and thus a new cell) for that i.

drills.q: When does `nonlocal x` raise a SyntaxError, and how is that different from what `global x` would do in the same situation?
drills.a: nonlocal x raises SyntaxError at compile time if no enclosing function scope already defines x — it never falls back to global. global x, by contrast, always succeeds, creating a module-level binding if one doesn't already exist.

drills.q: Explain mechanically why `def f(bucket=[]): bucket.append(x); return bucket` returns a growing list across unrelated calls.
drills.a: The default value [] is evaluated exactly once, when the def statement runs, and stored on the function object. Every call that doesn't pass its own bucket argument shares that same list object, so appends from unrelated calls accumulate in it.

drills.q: A class body defines `multiplier = 3` then `doubled = [v * multiplier for v in range(5)]`. Does this raise NameError? Explain using scope rules, and contrast with a plain for loop written directly in the class body.
drills.a: Yes, NameError: name 'multiplier' is not defined. A comprehension has its own scope which does not include the enclosing class body (only the outermost for-clause's iterable is evaluated in the class body's scope first). A plain for loop written directly in the class body, by contrast, executes in the class namespace itself and can see multiplier as a bare name.

drills.q: What is func.__closure__ and func.__code__.co_freevars, and how do they explain the shared-mutation behavior of nonlocal?
drills.a: __closure__ is a tuple of cell objects, one per free variable named in co_freevars. Each cell is a mutable box referenced by both the enclosing function's frame and the nested function; nonlocal x; x += 1 mutates that shared cell's contents in place, which is why the enclosing scope sees the change immediately.

drills.q: A loop spawns threads with `threading.Thread(target=lambda: worker(i)).start()` for i in range(5). Describe the failure mode and why it's worse than the single-threaded version of the same bug.
drills.a: All five lambdas close over the same shared cell for i. Because thread scheduling means the main loop typically finishes (and i reaches its final value) before the spawned threads actually invoke their lambdas, most or all threads end up calling worker with the same final value rather than their intended distinct index. It's worse than the single-threaded version because the exact outcome is timing-dependent — it can pass in testing and fail differently under production scheduling.

drills.q: Does Python 3.12's PEP 709 comprehension inlining change whether a comprehension's loop variable leaks into the enclosing scope? What did PEP 709 actually change?
drills.a: No, scoping is unchanged by design — the loop variable still does not leak. PEP 709 is a performance change: comprehensions are inlined into the enclosing frame instead of compiled as a separate nested function call, avoiding the overhead of a full function call and frame creation per comprehension, while preserving the existing scoping semantics.
